First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $-{90}^{∘}$ that lies in the range $[0,{360}^{∘}).$

$$
-{90}^{∘}+{360}^{∘}={270}^{∘}\,✓
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{csc}⁡(-{90}^{∘})=\operatorname{csc}⁡({270}^{∘}).$

The angle ${270}^{∘}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253609/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${270}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡({270}^{∘})=-1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡({270}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({270}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1.
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{csc}⁡(-{90}^{∘})=-1.$
